content: 1. Dance Interventions for Parkinson’s Disease: A study by Dos Santos Delabary (2018) reviewed five randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 159 participants, primarily men aged 61 to 72 years, across various stages of Parkinson’s disease (Hoehn & Yahr stages 0–4). Dance interventions, particularly tango classes, were conducted for at least three weeks. Participants in the dance groups showed improvements in motor symptoms (UPDRS III scale), functional mobility (TUG test), endurance (6MWT), freezing of gait (FOG-Q), and walking velocity (forward and backward) compared to no intervention or other forms of exercise. However, most differences were not statistically significant. The evidence was rated as moderate. 2. Nordic Walking for Parkinson’s Disease: Cugusi (2017) reviewed six RCTs with 221 participants aged 40 to 80 years, diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease for 5 to 7 years (Hoehn & Yahr stages 1–4). Nordic walking was compared to other exercise protocols or no exercise over 4 to 24 weeks. The evidence was rated as moderate. 3. Physical Activity and Cognitive Function in Parkinson’s Disease: Stuckenschneider (2019) reviewed 11 RCTs with 508 participants (mean age 68 years, Hoehn & Yahr stages 1–4). Interventions included aerobic, resistance, and coordination exercises lasting 4 to 26 weeks. Evidence on cognitive outcomes was mixed, with only one study showing significant improvement in global cognitive function, three showing effects on executive function, and none showing benefits for attention or processing speed. The evidence was rated as moderate. 4. Physical Activity for Stroke Survivors: Bonini-Rocha (2018) reviewed 11 RCTs with 750 participants aged 38 to 91 years, 1 to 157 months post-stroke. Circuit-based exercises (4 to 19 weeks, 2–7 sessions per week) improved walking function but had no significant effects on balance or functional mobility. The evidence was rated as moderate. 5. Tai Chi for Stroke Survivors: Li (2018) reviewed five RCTs with 346 participants aged 55 to 73 years. Tai Chi interventions (6 to 12 weeks) improved standing balance and gait ability compared to controls. The evidence was rated as low. 6. Pilates for Stroke Survivors: Miranda (2018) reviewed two RCTs with 39 participants aged 63 to 68 years. Pilates interventions improved functional status (TUG test), cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2 max), and balance compared to controls. The evidence was rated as moderate. 7. Dance for Stroke Survivors: Patterson (2018) reviewed three studies (two case reports, one before-after study) with 11 participants. Dance interventions (1 to 8 weeks) improved balance (Berg Balance Scale), but no statistical significance was reported. The evidence was rated as very low. 8. High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) for Stroke Survivors: Wiener (2019) reviewed three RCTs and three before-after studies with 140 participants. HIIT protocols (20–30 minutes per session, 2–5 times per week, for 2–8 weeks) improved cardiorespiratory fitness but showed no consistent effects on balance or functional mobility. The evidence was rated as low. 9. Traditional Chinese Exercises for Stroke Survivors: Zou (2018) reviewed 16 RCTs with 1,136 participants. Interventions included Tai Chi, Qigong, and yoga (4 to 12 weeks). Improvements were seen in walking function, but evidence was inconsistent and rated as very low. 10. Physical Activity for Major Depression: Limited evidence suggests that physical activity improves quality of life (QOL) in adults with major depression. Stubbs (2018) reviewed three RCTs, finding significant improvements in QOL with moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) but not with lower-intensity exercise. The evidence was rated as moderate. 11. Physical Activity for Schizophrenia: Stubbs (2018) reviewed three RCTs, finding that MVPA improved QOL and cognitive function (working memory, social cognition, attention/vigilance) in individuals with schizophrenia. However, no effects were observed for processing speed or verbal/visual memory. The evidence was rated as moderate. 12. Physical Activity for ADHD: Moderate evidence suggests that MVPA benefits cognitive function in individuals with ADHD, including improvements in attention and executive function. The evidence was rated as moderate. 13. Physical Activity for Spinal Cord Injury (SCI): Eitivipart (2019) reviewed 16 systematic reviews on aerobic fitness and muscle strength training for individuals with SCI. Despite low-quality evidence, recommendations suggest that ergometry training (20 minutes, moderate-to-vigorous intensity, twice weekly for six weeks) may improve aerobic fitness, while resistance training (three sets of 8–10 repetitions, moderate-to-vigorous intensity, twice weekly for six weeks) may improve muscle strength. 14. Physical Training for Upper Limb Strength in Paraplegia: Melo (2019) reviewed studies on physical training for upper limb strength in individuals with paraplegia. Positive effects were observed in activities of daily living and rehabilitation outcomes, particularly with resistance and combined training. In summary, physical activity interventions, including dance, Tai Chi, Pilates, and resistance training, show varying degrees of effectiveness in improving physical and cognitive outcomes across conditions such as Parkinson’s disease, stroke, depression, schizophrenia, ADHD, and SCI. However, the quality of evidence is often limited, and further research is needed to strengthen these findings.
